stories.headline: How the Mecca defense agreement works
stories.title: How the Mecca defense agreement works
stories.summary: Ankara: Turkey's government has asked parliament to ratify a mutual defense agreement it signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, bringing the country closer to bolstering Saudi defenses as it faces attacks from Iran-backed Houthi rebels.Mirroring NATO's Article 5, the so-called Mecca Joint Defense Agreement commits the sides to view an armed attack against one as an attack on all three.While Turkey says that it's considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, officials have cautioned that the pact is defensive in nature and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis.Turkish and Pakistani officials have also insisted that the pact isn't against Iran or any other country, but haven't said how they would react if attacked by Iran.Regional countries take responsibility for their securityThe agreement was signed in the Saudi holy city of Mecca in August by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif with the aim of increasing cooperation and deterrence among the three regional heavyweights at a time of increased uncertainty amid the Iran war.It brings together oil-rich Saudi Arabia and nuclear power Pakistan as well as Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a rapidly growing defense industry. It enables the three to take greater charge for their own security at a time of reduced U.S. involvement.For Pakistan, the Mecca Agreement builds on existing military ties with Riyadh. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a separate mutual defense agreement in September 2025.Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has repeatedly said that the Mecca agreement doesn't replace existing agreements and is open to other countries willing to uphold its principles and resolve differences peacefully.Nature of assistance planned is still unknownDuring an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month, the three countries agreed to immediately implement what they said were their collective defense commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia. They didn't elaborate.Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said that Turkey and Pakistan were assessing possible air defense, electronic warfare and technical assistance for Saudi Arabia."What type of assistance can be provided, especially in areas such as air defense and electronic warfare, what technical support can be offered? Work on these issues is ongoing," he said."Turkey will not be sending troops into another country's territory to carry out an attack. It is a defense agreement," Fidan said, addressing concerns raised by opposition parties that Turkey would be drawn into the conflict in Yemen.Authorities in Pakistan have declined to disclose deployment details, citing operational confidentiality. Officials say, however, that Pakistan's role would be strictly defensive. The Pakistani Information Ministry recently dismissed as "speculative" news reports that said Pakistan had already deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia.Comment from Saudi Arabia on the pact since the Houthi attacks has been limited. In a post on X following a visit by Pakistan's army chief, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman said: "We affirmed our commitment to continuing joint efforts to confront these attacks in accordance with the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense."10-year commitment to the pactLittle was known about the content of the pact until Turkey's government submitted it to parliament for approval on Tuesday.The 16-article agreement, published by Turkish state broadcaster TRT on its website, states that the countries would defend each other militarily in case of external aggression in line with the U.N. Charter's right of self-defense.The agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, including joint training programs, exercises and personnel exchanges. It allows cooperation in the defense industry, including joint weapons production and technology transfers as well as intelligence sharing.A surprise clause states that the parties wouldn't be able to withdraw from the pact for 10 years, after which they would need to provide a three-month notice to leave.A parliamentary committee is expected to review the agreement in the coming days before it reaches the Turkish parliament's general assembly for ratification. Separately, Turkey's parliament would have to authorize any deployment of Turkish military personnel.Pakistan's potential contributionsPakistan hasn't sought parliamentary endorsement of the Mecca agreement, but officials say the government and other national institutions support it. They say Islamabad would provide whatever military assistance Saudi Arabia needs to defend the kingdom and Islam's holiest sites.Pakistan's military has more than two decades of experience fighting militant groups, which analysts say could help it bolster Saudi defenses.The agreement builds on decades of Pakistani military service in Saudi Arabia. An unspecified number of Pakistani troops have been stationed in Saudi Arabia since the early 1980s to train and advise Saudi forces.Pact to be led by retired Pakistani generalEven before the ratification process has been completed, the three countries established and convened a meeting of the so-called Strategic Political and Defense Committee composed of the foreign ministers, defense ministers and chiefs of staff.The committee is expected to meet twice a year.The pact's secretariat will be based in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general. He will serve a three-year term.

opening: Ankara: Turkey's government has asked parliament to ratify a mutual defense agreement it signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, bringing the country closer to bolstering Saudi defenses as it faces attacks from Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Mirroring NATO's Article 5, the so-called Mecca Joint Defense Agreement commits the sides to view an armed attack against one as an attack on all three.
body: While Turkey says that it's considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, officials have cautioned that the pact is defensive in nature and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis.
Turkish and Pakistani officials have also insisted that the pact isn't against Iran or any other country, but haven't said how they would react if attacked by Iran.
Regional countries take responsibility for their security.

The agreement was signed in the Saudi holy city of Mecca in August by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif with the aim of increasing cooperation and deterrence among the three regional heavyweights at a time of increased uncertainty amid the Iran war.
It brings together oil-rich Saudi Arabia and nuclear power Pakistan as well as Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a rapidly growing defense industry.
It enables the three to take greater charge for their own security at a time of reduced U.S. involvement.
For Pakistan, the Mecca Agreement builds on existing military ties with Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a separate mutual defense agreement in September 2025.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has repeatedly said that the Mecca agreement doesn't replace existing agreements and is open to other countries willing to uphold its principles and resolve differences peacefully.
Nature of assistance planned is still unknown.

During an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month, the three countries agreed to immediately implement what they said were their collective defense commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.
They didn't elaborate.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said that Turkey and Pakistan were assessing possible air defense, electronic warfare and technical assistance for Saudi Arabia." What type of assistance can be provided, especially in areas such as air defense and electronic warfare, what technical support can be offered?
Work on these issues is ongoing," he said." Turkey will not be sending troops into another country's territory to carry out an attack.
It is a defense agreement," Fidan said, addressing concerns raised by opposition parties that Turkey would be drawn into the conflict in Yemen.
Authorities in Pakistan have declined to disclose deployment details, citing operational confidentiality.
The Pakistani Information Ministry recently dismissed as "speculative" news reports that said Pakistan had already deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia.
Comment from Saudi Arabia on the pact since the Houthi attacks has been limited.

In a post on X following a visit by Pakistan's army chief, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman said: "We affirmed our commitment to continuing joint efforts to confront these attacks in accordance with the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense."10-year commitment to the pactLittle was known about the content of the pact until Turkey's government submitted it to parliament for approval on Tuesday.

The 16-article agreement, published by Turkish state broadcaster TRT on its website, states that the countries would defend each other militarily in case of external aggression in line with the U.N. Charter's right of self-defense.
The agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, including joint training programs, exercises and personnel exchanges.
It allows cooperation in the defense industry, including joint weapons production and technology transfers as well as intelligence sharing.
A surprise clause states that the parties wouldn't be able to withdraw from the pact for 10 years, after which they would need to provide a three-month notice to leave.
A parliamentary committee is expected to review the agreement in the coming days before it reaches the Turkish parliament's general assembly for ratification.
Separately, Turkey's parliament would have to authorize any deployment of Turkish military personnel.
Pakistan's potential contributionsPakistan hasn't sought parliamentary endorsement of the Mecca agreement, but officials say the government and other national institutions support it.
They say Islamabad would provide whatever military assistance Saudi Arabia needs to defend the kingdom and Islam's holiest sites.
Pakistan's military has more than two decades of experience fighting militant groups, which analysts say could help it bolster Saudi defenses.
The agreement builds on decades of Pakistani military service in Saudi Arabia.
An unspecified number of Pakistani troops have been stationed in Saudi Arabia since the early 1980s to train and advise Saudi forces.

Pact to be led by retired Pakistani generalEven before the ratification process has been completed, the three countries established and convened a meeting of the so-called Strategic Political and Defense Committee composed of the foreign ministers, defense ministers and chiefs of staff.
The committee is expected to meet twice a year.
The pact's secretariat will be based in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general.
He will serve a three-year term.

stories.headline: Beyond telecom: Why investors may pay a premium for Jio's IPO
stories.title: Beyond telecom: Why investors may pay a premium for Jio's IPO
stories.summary: As Jio Platform’s initial public offering (IPO) opens for subscription on Wednesday, investors may not view it through the same lens as a traditional telecom offering. While Jio's market-leading mobile business provides scale and cash flows, the company's next phase of growth is expected to come from businesses beyond telecom.With much of its infrastructure already in place, Jio Platform is shifting its focus from network rollout to monetisation. The real investment bet goes well beyond subscriber additions, tariff increases, or market share gains. Instead, investors are betting on Jio's ability to unlock value from one of India's largest digital ecosystems, spanning artificial intelligence, cloud computing, enterprise technology, broadband and connected services.“Its future growth is expected to be supported by tariff rationalisation, migration from 2G to 4G and 5G, higher data consumption, home broadband expansion and increasing enterprise adoption of cloud and digital solutions,” analysts at SBI Securities say. They add that additional monetisation opportunities may emerge from AI-led services, digital applications, satellite connectivity, and overseas deployment of its proprietary technology platforms.The broader digital opportunity, rather than telecom earnings alone, is therefore what could justify a premium valuation for Jio Platform.Sudeep Anand, research analyst, Systematix also feels Jio Platforms is well placed to benefit from India’s accelerating digitalisation, supported by its large and diversified customer base, pan-India network and strong position in wireless data consumption.“Its integrated digital ecosystem spanning connectivity, broadband, digital platforms, cloud and enterprise services provides multiple avenues for sustained growth. Strong subscriber engagement, rising data usage, tariff-led average revenue per user (ARPU) expansion and increasing penetration of JioFiber and JioAirFiber should support revenue growth, while continued investments in ‘5G, AI and cloud infrastructure’ are expected to strengthen its technology leadership,” Anand explains.Anand elaborates that Jio Platforms offers an attractive opportunity to participate in India’s long-term digital and connectivity growth story.Also Read: Jio taps stock markets for Rs30,200 crore in landmark IPO“While elevated capex requirements, competitive intensity, regulatory interventions and execution risks remain key monitorable, the company’s market leadership, robust profitability, strong cash-generation profile and multiple structural growth levers provide comfort on its long-term prospects,” he adds.Why are markets paying attention?Ahead of its IPO for the public subscription, the company has already raised Rs 8,109.84 crore from 212 anchor investors. Some marquee global investors in the anchor book include like BlackRock, Capital Group, Fidelity Investments, T. Rowe Price, Schroders, JPMorgan Asset Management, Franklin Templeton, Invesco, and Prudential.The three-day sale will close for subscription on October 23. The offering comprises a fresh issue of 27 crore shares. The Mukesh Ambani-led company aims to raise around Rs 30,200 crore with a price band set at Rs 1,065-1,119 per piece, positioning it among the biggest IPOs ever in India.Jio Platforms' Rs 30,200-crore offering is an entirely fresh issue, which means existing shareholders will not sell any shares through the IPO; instead, the entire proceeds will be used by the company. A large part of the funds—up to Rs 27,500 crore—will be used to pare debt at Reliance Jio Infocomm, while the balance will support general corporate requirements and future growth initiatives.Jio Platforms is India’s largest digital-connectivity platform, with operations spanning mobile and fixed broadband, enterprise connectivity and digital services.Through Reliance Jio Infocomm, Jio Platforms was the first operator in India to launch a standalone 5G network and has supported rapid adoption of 5G services across the country. As of 1QFY27, the company had 284.9 million 5G customers, representing the third-largest 5G customer base globally. Its 5G network supports applications such as ultra-high-definition and 4K video streaming, cloud gaming, augmented reality and virtual reality.Over the years, Jio Platforms has attracted a range of bluechip global investors, including Meta, Google, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, KKR-backed Omicron Asia Holdings, General Atlantic Singapore, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority-backed Platinum Jasmine, and TPG-managed India Markets. However, Reliance Industries continues to hold a controlling 66.43 percent stake in the company, retaining a firm grip over the group's most valuable digital asset.Valuation gameAccording to analysts at Geojit Investments, at the upper price band of the IPO, Jio is valued at 15 times FY26 enterprise value (EV)/EBITDA on a post-issue basis, implying a premium to industry peers. “This premium is justified by Jio’s market leadership, improving monetisation, strong cash flow generation, and substantial long-term optionality beyond its core telecom business,” they say.The analysts explain that the IPO-led deleveraging is expected to further strengthen the balance sheet. While the near- term upside may be moderated by the premium valuation, the monetisation of cloud, AI, enterprise solutions, entertainment, digital platforms, and fixed broadband services could emerge as key drivers of earnings growth over the medium to long term.The company benefits from a dominant position in India's mobile broadband market with 533.3 million customers, approximately 49.8 percent wireless broadband market share. Its proprietary technology stack, extensive distribution network and strong brand franchise provide significant competitive advantages and create high barriers to entry, says Rinkle Vira, analyst at Anand Rathi.“Considering its leadership position in India's digital ecosystem, strong profitability, scalable technology platform, robust growth prospects and significant opportunities in AI, enterprise digital services and fixed broadband, the valuation appears reasonable relative to its long-term growth potential,” Vira explains.Also Read: Telecom tariffs back in focus as Airtel and Jio take divergent pathsIndia has a four-player mobile market, and the top three players have a mobile broadband market share of over 97 percent as of June 30, 2026. Jio is themarket leader, followed by Bharti Airtel at 35.47 percent, Vodafone Idea at 12.51 percent and BSNL at 2.20 percent.As of June, Jio also holds the industry’s largest spectrum bank, totalling 26,800.8 MHz, with a 16-year average remaining life. Jio is the only operator in India to have spectrum in low-band, mid-band and millimetre wave (700 MHz, 3300 MHz and 26 GHz) for 5G across all circles.Jio is the first operator in India to launch a standalone 5G network, which operates independently of 4G infrastructure and has advanced capabilities like network slicing and superior low-latency performance. Jio has the third-largest 5G customer base in the world, with 284.9 million customers on 5G as of June. Its standalone architecture across bands supports this scale, delivering average speeds of 198.9 Mbps in Q3 FY2026.“At 33 times FY2026 earnings, valuation is at the lower end versus peers,” say analysts at Canara Securities. They see Jio benefiting from volume-led growth across its mobility, home, and MSME businesses, while bundled media, productivity, and AI solutions provide a clear pathway to ARPU improvement.According to analysts at Shriram Research, at the upper price band, the issue is valued reasonably, which is well-supported by Jio's undisputed market leadership and consistent double- digit EBITDA growth. “The company stands out as a core structural compounder for India's digital economy, underpinned by robust cash generation, declining leverage as IPO proceeds are utilised to repay debt, and rapid adoption of home broadband services,” they say.According to analysts at Shriram Research, Jio Platform's revenue and profitability are poised for sustained expansion, driven by ongoing ARPU hikes, 2G-to-4G/5G subscriber migration, deepening enterprise relationships, and the potential export of its proprietary in-house tech stack to overseas operators.“While regulatory and competitive risks remain, the structural health of the industry and the strength of an integrated digital ecosystem make this an attractive, high-conviction opportunity for medium- to long-term investors,” analysts at Shriram Research add.Part of the Reliance ecosystemFollowing Jio’s listing, Reliance Industries will be India’s largest listed conglomerate, marking a formal generational transition to children Akash, Anant, and Isha Ambani under chairman Mukesh Ambani’s guidance. Reliance Industries met Mukesh Ambani’s 2019 target of becoming net debt-free by 2021 despite the Covid-19 pandemic. The shares of RIL have delivered a 29 percent annualised shareholder return since its 1977 IPO.Meanwhile, celebrating a decade since its launch on September 6, 2026, Jio has grown into India's largest digital connectivity platform, with a customer base of 53 crore with a 60 percent share of India's data traffic.Jio completed India’s nationwide 4G-to-5G standalone migration in 19 months, creating the world’s largest 5G subscriber base outside China at 284.9 million, while users consume 43.7 GB monthly, which is 1.5 times that of the nearest competitor. Since Jio’s 2016 launch, the telecom market has consolidated from 14 to four operators, data prices have fallen from Rs 228 per GB to Rs 7.50 per GB, and speeds have surged from 2.5 Mbps to 68 Mbps.Over FY2024-FY2026, its revenue grew at a 15.8 percent CAGR to Rs 1.47 lakh crore, EBITDA rose 17 percent while net profit jumped 18.43 percent to Rs 30,064 crore.“At the upper price band, the issue is valued at a post-issue FY26 price-to-earnings (PE) multiple of 34.4 times and an enterprise value/subscriber multiple of Rs 20,117, reflecting its scale, earnings growth, technology capabilities and long-term monetisation potential,” say analysts at SBI Securities.As of June, the company and its subsidiaries have applied for 7,220 patents across 4G, 5G, and 6G cloud-native core network architectures, AI-driven network automation, and other digital technologies. This portfolio includes 2,655 patent applications in India and 4,565 filed in international jurisdictions.

The analysts explain that the IPO-led deleveraging is expected to further strengthen the balance sheet.

While the near- term upside may be moderated by the premium valuation, the monetisation of cloud, AI, enterprise solutions, entertainment, digital platforms, and fixed broadband services could emerge as key drivers of earnings growth over the medium to long term.

Its proprietary technology stack, extensive distribution network and strong brand franchise provide significant competitive advantages and create high barriers to entry, says Rinkle Vira, analyst at Anand Rathi.

stories.headline: India and the digital quarter-century
stories.title: India and the digital quarter-century
stories.summary: At my first posting in 1977, banking meant handwritten scrolls, ledgers and sheets of carbon paper. I wrote so much that I developed corn on my finger. Today, a street vendor can receive a QR-code payment before the customer has put away the phone. Few contrasts capture India’s transformation more vividly.This is not principally a banking story. It is the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.From a Large Economy to a Connected OneIn 2000, India’s gross domestic product was about $468 billion. By 2025, it had risen to nearly $3.96 trillion in current-dollar terms, according to the World Bank data. At the end of 2025, India also had more than one billion broadband subscriptions, according to TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India).Connectivity has reduced the cost of distance. A small enterprise can reach customers nationally without first building a national physical network; a migrant worker can transfer money home instantly; and an entrepreneur can begin with cloud software rather than heavy infrastructure. By December 2025, India had more than 2.07 lakh recognised startups, which reported creating over 21.9 lakh direct jobs, according to DPIIT (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade).The business environment remains a work in progress. Digitising a complicated process does not automatically make it simple. Yet online systems for taxation, company filings, procurement and enterprise registration have widened participation in the formal economy and made markets more accessible.Also Read: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governanceGovernment as a Builder of Digital RailsThe government’s most consequential role has not been to create every digital service. It has been to establish identity, payment and data rails on which public institutions and private businesses can build.Aadhaar, Jan Dhan, mobile connectivity, UPI and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) emerged through coordination among government, regulators, banks, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), technology companies and frontline workers. Policy continuity mattered, as did the preference for interoperable infrastructure rather than isolated, closed systems.The scale is remarkable. As of August 5, the Jan Dhan programme had 58.97 crore beneficiaries; 32.86 crore were women and 45.86 crore were served through rural and semi-urban branches. In FY24–25, UPI processed 185.9 billion transactions worth about ₹260.6 lakh crore. The DBT platform reports cumulative transfers of nearly ₹52.96 lakh crore.These figures illustrate a distinctive Indian model. Government helped build common rails and established trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility. The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation.Reaching the Last MileMy years in banking gave me a front-row seat to this transition, but they also taught me not to confuse a digital launch with a social outcome. An account opened is not necessarily an account used. An application is not inclusive if the customer lacks connectivity, confidence, language support or a reliable way to resolve a problem.In branches and rural communities, I saw that technology worked best when paired with human assistance—business correspondents, self-help groups, trained employees and trusted local institutions. Digital infrastructure should not simply remove people from processes. It should free people from routine work so they can focus on advice, credit, enterprise and problem-solving.That is why grassroots adoption remains central. India’s next phase must invest in digital literacy, accessible design and assisted channels, particularly for women, small farmers, micro-enterprises, older citizens and first-time users.Also Read: Unleashing India's potential over 25 yearsCovid-19: A National Stress TestCovid-19 caused enormous human and economic suffering, but it also revealed the value of India’s digital foundations. Payments, benefit transfers, remote work, online commerce and digital public services became instruments of continuity almost overnight.I had earlier tried to introduce a work-from-home option in banking, especially for employees managing care responsibilities. opening: At my first posting in 1977, banking meant handwritten scrolls, ledgers and sheets of carbon paper.
I wrote so much that I developed corn on my finger.
body: Today, a street vendor can receive a QR-code payment before the customer has put away the phone.
Few contrasts capture India’s transformation more vividly.
This is not principally a banking story.
It is the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.
From a Large Economy to a Connected.
In 2000, India’s gross domestic product was about $468 billion.
By 2025, it had risen to nearly $3.96 trillion in current-dollar terms, according to the World Bank data.
At the end of 2025, India also had more than one billion broadband subscriptions, according to TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India).
Connectivity has reduced the cost of distance.

A small enterprise can reach customers nationally without first building a national physical network; a migrant worker can transfer money home instantly; and an entrepreneur can begin with cloud software rather than heavy infrastructure.
By December 2025, India had more than 2.07 lakh recognised startups, which reported creating over 21.9 lakh direct jobs, according to DPIIT (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade).
The business environment remains a work in progress.
Digitising a complicated process does not automatically make it simple.
Yet online systems for taxation, company filings, procurement and enterprise registration have widened participation in the formal economy and made markets more accessible.
Government as a Builder of Digital Rails.
The government’s most consequential role has not been to create every digital service.
It has been to establish identity, payment and data rails on which public institutions and private businesses can build.

Aadhaar, Jan Dhan, mobile connectivity, UPI and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) emerged through coordination among government, regulators, banks, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), technology companies and frontline workers.
Policy continuity mattered, as did the preference for interoperable infrastructure rather than isolated, closed systems.
The scale is remarkable.
As of August 5, the Jan Dhan programme had 58.97 crore beneficiaries; 32.86 crore were women and 45.86 crore were served through rural and semi-urban branches.
In FY24–25, UPI processed 185.9 billion transactions worth about ₹260.6 lakh crore.
The DBT platform reports cumulative transfers of nearly ₹52.96 lakh crore.
These figures illustrate a distinctive Indian model.
Government helped build common rails and established trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility.
The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation.
Reaching the Last MileMy years in banking gave me a front-row seat to this transition, but they also taught me not to confuse a digital launch with a social outcome.
An account opened is not necessarily an account used.
An application is not inclusive if the customer lacks connectivity, confidence, language support or a reliable way to resolve a problem.
In branches and rural communities, I saw that technology worked best when paired with human assistance—business correspondents, self-help groups, trained employees and trusted local institutions.
Digital infrastructure should not simply remove people from processes.
It should free people from routine work so they can focus on advice, credit, enterprise and problem-solving.
That is why grassroots adoption remains central.
India’s next phase must invest in digital literacy, accessible design and assisted channels, particularly for women, small farmers, micro-enterprises, older citizens and first-time users.
Covid-19: A National Stress TestCovid-19 caused enormous human and economic suffering, but it also revealed the value of India’s digital foundations.
Payments, benefit transfers, remote work, online commerce and digital public services became instruments of continuity almost overnight.
I had earlier tried to introduce a work-from-home option in banking, especially for employees managing care responsibilities.
It encountered resistance because physical presence was often confused with productivity.
The pandemic overturned that assumption.
When I moved into enterprise technology in 2020, I watched organisations compress years of digital change into months.
At the national level, CoWIN provided scheduling, stock tracking and verifiable certificates for a vaccination programme that had administered more than 220 crore doses by January 2023.
India also offered the platform as an open-source digital public good to other countries.
It showed that software built for Indian scale could have global relevance.
From Indian Innovation to a Global Reference.

India’s digital public infrastructure is now studied internationally because it offers a model in which the state creates foundational, interoperable systems and public and private providers innovate above them.

A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.
India’s global contribution is, therefore, larger than any single platform.
It is the demonstration that population-scale systems can be designed as shared infrastructure.
The corresponding responsibility is to ensure that openness and speed are matched by cybersecurity, privacy, consumer protection and accountable governance.
Women form the majority in all of Jan Dhan accounts.
And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts.
Photo by Idrees Mohammed / AFPTurning Access into Agency.
The past 25 years have changed my understanding of technology.
I once saw it largely as a means of automating processes.
I now see it as an operating system for economic participation.
The next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive.
But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement.
The government must continue to provide enabling infrastructure and clear rules, while enterprise competes, innovates and invests responsibly.
India has built an extraordinary infrastructure of access.

The test of the next 25 years is whether that access becomes agency: Whether a farmer receives timely credit, a woman entrepreneur reaches a national market, a small business uses AI productively, and every citizen can participate in growth with dignity.
That is when digital transformation becomes national transformation.

A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.
And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts.

stories.headline: Supreme Court judgment opens up the religion-neutrality of OBC classification for debate
stories.title: Supreme Court judgment opens up the religion-neutrality of OBC classification for debate
stories.summary: The Supreme Court clarifies that non-Hindu communities can be OBC, but distinguishes between the sources of backwardness for Hindu OBCs and non-Hindu OBCs on the question of continuing backwardness for converts
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

event term: 'supreme court judgment' in title weight 46

article_sentences: The religion-neutrality of the Other Backward Classes (OBC) classification has been thrown open for debate after the Supreme Court’s recent decision that an OBC Hindu person loses the entitlement to reservation once they convert to another religion.

While the Scheduled Castes (SCs) have always been identified by a religion criterion, and the Scheduled Tribes (STs) classification has never considered religion, and the OBC classification, since its implementation after the 1992 Indra Sawhneyvs.
Union of India judgment, has remained religion-neutral.
Communities (whether classes or castes) are examined for 11 social, educational, and economic backwardness indicators, and then classified as such based on a threshold score.
Forms for OBC certificates across States do not ask for the religion of an applicant nor does an OBC certificate declare the holder’s religion.

In deciding the question of whether a Hindu OBC person is entitled to reservation after converting to another faith, the Supreme Court Bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar, in its October 15 judgment, has established that the “source of social backwardness” must necessarily be considered in this inquiry.
The judgment noted that, for a Hindu OBC individual, the “legal foundation” of their entitlement to reservation is “specifically conditioned upon membership of that Hindu social order”.
Discussing the “source of social backwardness”, the court noted that while Indra Sawhneyvs.

Union of India prevented caste from being the sole criterion for OBC classification, what cannot be disregarded is that in Hindu society, the “foundational institution” of caste has historically determined social and other manifestations of backwardness.

While the court admitted in the judgment that educational, economic, and other forms of backwardness may continue for an OBC person who has left the Hindu faith, their very act of choosing another faith puts them in a different “social order”, altering the “source of social backwardness”, it has said.

This reading of the Bench of Justices Mishra and Chandrashekhar flows from how it has understood the idea of social stratification across faiths in India, essentially noting that the source of social backwardness varies based on the nature of social stratification in any given social order.

This understanding of social stratification makes a subtle departure from how the same concept was discussed in the Indra Sawhney judgment, which has laid the foundation for identifying OBCs so far, without entering the question of the source of social backwardness, regardless of whether the communities are classes or castes, Hindu or Muslim.

stories.headline: December MPC meet: A 50 bps repo hike vs 25 bps hike with a wider LAF corridor? SBI Research on two RBI options
stories.title: December MPC meet: A 50 bps repo hike vs 25 bps hike with a wider LAF corridor? SBI Research on two RBI options
stories.summary: SBI Research has outlined two possible ways for the RBI to tighten monetary policy in December: a 50 bps repo rate hike or a 25 bps hike combined with an asymmetric adjustment to the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) corridor.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'repo rate' in summary weight 25.2
event term: 'monetary policy' in summary weight 24
article_sentences: What are the two options proposed by SBI Research?
Under the first, conventional option, SBI Research proposes raising the repo rate by 50 bps from the current 5.50% to 6.00%.
Under this scenario, the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate would be 6.25%, while the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate would be 5.75%.
The second option combines a smaller repo rate increase with a change in the liquidity corridor.
Under this proposal, the repo rate would rise by 25 bps to 5.75%, while the MSF rate would be set at 6.25% and the SDF rate at 5.50%.
This would create an asymmetric LAF corridor, with a wider gap between the repo rate and the two standing facility rates.
SBI Research says such an approach could be considered amid global uncertainty and the need to maintain orderly market functioning.
How does the LAF corridor work?
The LAF corridor helps guide short-term money-market rates around the RBI's policy rate.
The repo rate is the rate at which banks borrow funds from the RBI against eligible securities.
The SDF allows banks to deposit surplus funds with the central bank, while the MSF enables eligible banks to obtain overnight liquidity at a rate above the repo rate.
Changes to these rates influence the cost and availability of short-term funds in the banking system.

stories.headline: Supreme Court stalls Andhra Pradesh civic poll candidate list until October 25
stories.title: Supreme Court stalls Andhra Pradesh civic poll candidate list until October 25
stories.summary: Supreme Court stalls Andhra Pradesh civic poll candidate list until October 25
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The Supreme Court told the Andhra Pradesh poll panel to examine YSRCP complaints.
The directions underscore that secure nomination filing is integral to free and fair elections.
A vacation bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing a petition filed by the Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party, or YSRCP.
The party alleged that violence and threats had prevented several of its candidates from filing nomination papers for elections to around 100 urban local bodies.

The bench directed the state election commission to consider complaints submitted by the YSRCP and other candidates, along with supporting material, and decide by Thursday whether to extend the nomination deadline.
It also asked the commission to take all necessary steps to address concerns among the YSRCP and other candidates about free and fair elections in the state.
The court directed the Andhra Pradesh Director General of Police to provide adequate security to candidates and election offices.
It observed that the filing of nomination papers was an essential part of free and fair elections.
The bench clarified that it was not directly intervening in the election process but was allowing the state election commission to consider the party's complaint and take an appropriate decision.
It asked the commission to file a compliance affidavit by October 27, the next date of hearing.
According to PTI, the court said the YS Jagan Mohan Reddy-led party had “made out prima facie case” that several of its candidates had been stopped from filing nomination papers.
The court referred to representations submitted by the party and its candidates, both physically and electronically, as well as video clips and other electronic evidence.
